idea: When to replace old plumbing pipes
title: Internal Corrosion in Galvanized Iron Water Pipes
description: Old galvanized steel water pipes often look intact from the outside while failing internally. Over years of service, oxygen and dissolved minerals react with steel to form heavy internal rust deposits, a process called tuberculation. This build-up severely restricts water flow, lowering fixture pressure and causing periodic water discoloration. Because tuberculation eats away at the pipe wall material itself, chemical flushing or descaling cannot restore the pipe and often triggers pinhole leaks. When internal diameter restriction reaches this level, replacing the affected run with modern code-compliant piping like PPR, PEX, or copper is the correct solution.

The internal bore of the pipe is heavily choked with real rust, mineral scale, and tuberculation layer, drastically reducing the inner diameter while the outer pipe wall shows minor surface oxidation. The pipe is held in a professional plumber's gloved hand at a bright, clean residential utility work area. The background is softly blurred showing organized hand tools on a workbench. High detail on metal rust texture and pipe wall cross-section. Realistic physical geometry, photorealistic style, crisp focus on the pipe core, uncluttered top and bottom areas for text overlay. No text, no visual overlays, no logos, no watermarks, no fake labels.
visual_story: The visual visualizes why old pipes must be replaced even when they aren't visibly leaking on the outside. Viewers immediately see a cross-section of an old galvanized pipe where internal rust build-up (tuberculation) has choked off over 70% of the internal flow path. This directly connects the physical reality inside the pipe to common symptoms like persistent low water pressure and rusty water.

on_image_text.hook: Low water pressure isn't always a faulty valve.
on_image_text.explanation: Galvanized steel pipes corrode internally over time, creating rust build-up that chokes water flow.
on_image_text.takeaway: When internal rust restricts pipe volume, flushing won't fix it—replacement is necessary.
